newsitem.title: UK: UK funds wary on EMU date, see strategy moves - poll.
newsitem.headline: UK funds wary on EMU date, see strategy moves - poll.

text.p: Almost two-thirds of UK fund managers said European economic and monetary union (EMU) would significantly change their investment plans, but almost an equal number expect the start date for the single currency to be postponed, a monthly survey showed.
A majority of continental European fund managers, meantime, believe EMU will take place on time and only a third said it would change their investment plans.

The monthly Gallup poll of fund managers for U.S. investment house Merrill Lynch said 62 percent of UK managers believed EMU would significantly change their investments. Only 32 percent of continental European fund managers agreed to the same statement.

As much as 60 percent of UK fund managers said the planned EMU start date of January 1, 1999 will be postponed while about half that, 32 percent, of continental managers said a delay in the timetable is likely.
The Merrill/Gallup survey polled 67 UK-based fund managers with combined assets worth $1,470 billion. It polled 60 continental managers with assests totalling $514 billion.

Elsewhere, the survey showed only 22 percent of UK managers believed Britain would never join EMU while only 13 percent of their European counterparts saw the UK remaining outside the single currency indefinitely.

Even fewer UK fund managers, just six percent, said monetary union would not take place at all, even though 16 percent of continental managers said they thought EMU was unlikely to get off the ground.
Regarding the success of the currency, about half of UK and continental funds managers polled agreed that the euro will be "hard" rather than "soft."
More than 90 percent of the UK managers expected Germany, France and the Benelux countries to start in the first wave of EMU but only 10-12 percent expected Italy, Spain and Sweden to do likewise.

Expectations among continental managers were broadly similar but a slightly higher proportion, about 20 percent, believed Italy and Sweden would be there at the start and 38 percent thought Spain would make it on time.
